title: Storage & Search Handbook: Object Stores to Elasticsearch
summary: Quick revision notes on block, file and object storage, S3 mechanics (presigned URLs, multipart upload, tiers), data lakes vs warehouses, and search with inverted indexes, Elasticsearch, relevance and database sync.

chapters.title: Storage Types: Block, File, Object
points: Block storage: raw fixed-size blocks attached to one server as a disk (EBS); lowest latency, used for databases and boot volumes
File storage: hierarchical directories with POSIX locking, shared over NFS/SMB (EFS); good for shared home dirs and legacy apps
Object storage: flat namespace of key + immutable blob + metadata, accessed over HTTP (S3); scales to billions of objects, cheap, high latency
Objects are replaced whole, not edited in place: changing one byte means re-uploading the object; no append or rename (rename = copy + delete)
Pick by access pattern: random small writes → block, shared mutable files → file, big write-once media/backups/logs → object

chapters.title: S3 Core: Buckets, Keys, Consistency
points: Bucket names are globally unique; an object is bucket + key; folders are only a key-prefix convention (photos/2026/a.jpg), listing by prefix with delimiter '/' fakes directories
Single object max 50 TB (raised from 5 TB in Dec 2025); one PUT max 5 GB, so anything larger must use multipart
S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for PUT, overwrite and DELETE, plus list-after-write
Everyday CLI: aws s3 cp file s3://b/key, aws s3 sync dir s3://b/prefix, aws s3 ls s3://b/prefix/, aws s3 rm s3://b/key --recursive
Mistakes: public buckets (keep Block Public Access on), hot sequential key names assumed to throttle (prefixes scale at 3500 PUT / 5500 GET per second each), no versioning so overwrites are lost

chapters.title: Presigned URLs and Multipart Upload
points: Presigned URL: a URL signed with your credentials that grants one operation (GET or PUT) on one key until it expires; the holder needs no AWS credentials

Browser-direct upload flow: client asks backend → backend signs PUT URL → client uploads straight to S3, so file bytes never pass through your server; code: s3.generate_presigned_url('put_object', Params={'Bucket':b,'Key':k}, ExpiresIn=900)

The URL dies early if the signing credentials are temporary (an IAM role's session token expires first); the signer needs the permission itself; PUT URLs must match the signed Content-Type if it was included
Multipart upload: initiate → upload parts in parallel (each 5 MB–5 GB, up to 10,000 parts) → complete with the ETag list; use above ~100 MB, required above 5 GB; failed parts retry individually
Mistake: abandoned incomplete multipart uploads keep billing for stored parts invisibly; add a lifecycle rule AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload after 7 days

chapters.title: Storage Tiers, Lifecycle, Lakes and Warehouses
points: S3 tiers by access frequency: Standard (hot) → Standard-IA / One Zone-IA (infrequent, retrieval fee, 30-day minimum, 128 KB minimum billed) → Glacier Instant → Glacier Flexible (minutes–hours restore) → Deep Archive (12h+ restore, cheapest)
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers automatically by access pattern for a small monitoring fee; best when access is unpredictable
Lifecycle rule example: transition logs/ to IA at 30 days, Glacier at 90, expire at 365; the rule also expires old noncurrent versions
Data lake: raw data of any format kept in object storage, schema applied on read (schema-on-read), queried with Athena/Spark; cheap and flexible but can rot into a swamp without a catalog

Data warehouse: structured, modeled tables with schema-on-write, columnar and fast for SQL analytics (Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake); costlier; lakehouse formats (Iceberg, Delta) add table features onto lake files

chapters.title: Inverted Indexes and Elasticsearch Basics
points: Inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it (term → [doc ids]), so search looks up terms instead of scanning every document; LIKE '%word%' cannot use a normal B-tree index

Analysis pipeline at index and query time: character filters → tokenizer → token filters (lowercase, stopwords, stemming: 'running' → 'run'); mismatched analyzers at index vs query time cause missing hits

Elasticsearch: documents (JSON) live in an index split into primary shards, each with replicas; node count and shard count are chosen up front, since primary shard count cannot change without reindexing
Everyday queries: GET /products/_search with match (analyzed full text), term (exact, for keyword fields), bool with must / filter / should / must_not, plus range, sort, from/size

Mistakes: dynamic mapping guesses wrong types (set explicit mappings; text vs keyword), deep pagination with from+size (use search_after), too many tiny shards, treating Elasticsearch as the primary database

chapters.title: Relevance, Search Sync and Cheat Sheet
points: Relevance scoring uses BM25: higher for rare terms (IDF), more occurrences in the doc (TF, with saturation), and shorter fields; boost fields like title^3 and use multi_match to combine fields; filter clauses skip scoring and get cached
Sync pattern 1, dual write from app code: simple but a crash between the two writes leaves them diverged and gives no ordering guarantee

Sync pattern 2, change data capture (Debezium reading the DB log → Kafka → indexer) or an outbox table: reliable, ordered, replayable; the database stays the source of truth and the index is rebuildable

Make indexing idempotent: use the DB primary key as the document _id and the row version as external versioning, so retries and out-of-order events cannot overwrite newer data; search is near-real-time (refresh ~1s), so reads right after a write may miss it

Cheat sheet: block = disk, file = shared tree, object = HTTP blobs; presign for direct uploads, multipart above 100 MB with abort lifecycle; tier by access with lifecycle rules; lake = raw schema-on-read, warehouse = modeled schema-on-write; inverted index = term → docs; text for search, keyword for exact; DB is truth, index is derived
